results.title: Australia, Vietnam boost military ties with eye on China
results.description: SYDNEY, Australia — Australia and Vietnam said on Tuesday they would expand cooperation between their militaries as the middle powers face down Beijing’s expanding reach in the Pacific and the South China Sea. Following talks between Prime Minister Anthony Albanese and Vietnamese President To Lam in the Australian capital Canberra, the two countries said their defense forces would work more closely together on maritime security and conduct joint training. “Our defense industries, as well as our defense forces, are cooperating more and more,” Albanese said in opening remarks as he met with the Vietnamese leader. “Today’s uncertain world means that it is more important than ever that friends engage with each other on all levels — economic, social, environmental — to meet the challenges that are before us,” he added. The Vietnamese leader’s visit to Australia comes as both countries chafe against a growing military build-up by China in the region. Vietnam is one of a number of nations with competing claims in the South China Sea, which Beijing claims in nearly its entirety despite an international ruling that its assertion has no legal basis. Australia is also overseeing a once-in-a-generation expansion of its defense forces and a growing United States military footprint on its territory in a bid to counter Beijing’s buildup of forces. Australia’s Defense Minister Richard Marles said on Tuesday the deepening cooperation with Vietnam would “directly contribute to the stability and security of our region.” Tuesday’s announcement came alongside a slate of deals between Canberra and Hanoi, including a commitment to deepen “economic resilience,” as well as restart market access for Australian game meat — including kangaroo — to Vietnam.

results.title: Wolverine-Themed PlayStation 5 Consoles And Controllers Drop In September
results.description: Marvel's Wolverine, one of the biggest games of the year, comes out it a little over a month. Today we learned it'll get the same treatment as PlayStation's other beloved first-party IP and launch alongside a limited edition PS5 console and controller. A bundle with a PS5 digital edition (there's no disc drive – more on that later), controller, and a game code for Marvel's Wolverine will be available starting September 15, the same day as the game comes out. Check it out for yourself below. The console and controller feature a slashing design caused by Wolverine's iconic claws, and the console itself includes art of Wolverine's face. For those who already have a PS5, PlayStation is also selling console covers, which you can swap out for the system's base white plates (or whatever color you might have on there now). The covers will get an added color, Adamantium, which swaps out the yellow for silver, but while there are yellow covers for both the PS5 Slim and PS5 Pro, you can only get Adamantium for a PS5 pro. Controllers will come in both colors, however. The bundle and yellow controller will be available at "select retailers," but the console covers and silver controller are exclusive to PlayStation's online storefront . All of these products have, unsurprisingly, been affected by Sony's recent string of price increases for its physical hardware and accessories. Here's how much each item is going to cost: PlayStation 5 Digital Edition – Marvel’s Wolverine Battle Yellow Limited Edition Bundle: $649.99 US / £569.99 GBP/ €649.99 EUR / ¥96,980 JPY DualSense Wireless Controller – Marvel’s Wolverine Battle Yellow Limited Edition: $84.99 US / £74.99 GBP/ €84.99 EUR / ¥12,480 JPY PlayStation 5 Console Covers – Battle Yellow Limited Edition: $74.99 US / £64.99 GBP / €74.99 EUR / ¥9,980 JPY PlayStation 5 Pro Console Covers – Marvel’s Wolverine Battle Yellow Limited Edition: $74.99 US / £64.99 GBP/ €74.99 EUR / ¥9,980 JPY PlayStation 5 Pro Console Covers –Marvel’s Wolverine Adamantium Limited Edition: $74.99 US / £64.99 GBP / €74.99 EUR DualSense Wireless Controller – Marvel’s Wolverine Adamantium Limited Edition: $84.99 US / £74.99 GBP/ €84.99 EUR Of course, this all comes during a controversial time for PlayStation. Its decision to phase out physical disc releases starting in 2028 has frustrated fans around the world, and the comments of the video linked above are flooded with people complaining about the company's decision and the bundled console's lack of a disc drive. Even unrelated videos on the channel, like trailers for third-party games coming to PS5 have their comments full of people standing up for physical discs. At the same time, physical media is undeniably becoming more expensive to produce, and PlayStation has raised the price of its consoles and accessories twice in the last year – first last August , then this March . For more Wolverine, you can check out this trailer showcasing Lady Deathstrike or this interview revealing the game takes place before the X-Men exist . For more on our frustrations around rising prices and our frustrations with gaming's biggest companies, read executive editor Brian Shea's opinion piece about why the most recent console generation has been a "race to the bottom."

results.title: A country of winners, governed like losers
results.description: I JUST watched Alex Eala lose to Belinda Bencic a few minutes ago as I write this, and it occurred to me that her loss could provide the perfect coda to my three-part examination of our domestic political dynamics: “The Philippines — strong people, weak state”; “The president we keep waiting for”; and “Why institutions never outgrow presidents.” The theme running through all three is simple: the Filipinos are a great people shortchanged by their political leadership. The Filipino is not the problem We are a nation whose people excel abroad in almost every human endeavor, particularly in countries where competence and merit are rewarded and institutions are stronger than personalities. Alex is my exemplar. But so are millions of OFWs who leave their families behind and discover in foreign lands that Filipinos can compete with the best when the playing field is reasonably level and the rules actually mean something. And then they come home. They return to a country whose political system too often negates the very qualities that allow them to flourish elsewhere: merit, discipline, accountability and respect for rules. When Alex came home a fortnight ago to receive the adulation of Filipinos and the praises of our president and government, there was an irony we perhaps failed to notice. Outside Malacañang, the country was watching another great political confrontation, in the hallowed halls of the Senate, no less — making a mockery of a constitutional assertion — senator/judges in an impeachment proceedings performing as partisan prosecutors and defense lawyers. Inside Malacañang, it was celebrating a young Filipino whose rise was built on discipline, merit and measurable performance. Two very different Philippine stories occurring almost simultaneously. We honored a young Filipino woman whose success was built upon precisely those qualities our political system has difficulty rewarding. Nobody gave Alex a tennis match because of her surname. No political patron could appoint her into the quarterfinals. No dynasty could inherit her ranking. No padrino could negotiate away a double fault. The umpire does not ask which family you belong to before making the call. You perform — or you lose. If only our Republic is run that way. While the country was cheering For while we feted Alex, Filipinos elsewhere were again wading through floodwaters and asking familiar questions about flood control projects, contractors and missing accountability. Our political leaders, meanwhile, were doing what they do exceedingly well: fighting one another. The nation is consumed by the impeachment battle surrounding VP Sara. Alliances are being assembled and dismantled. Accusations fly. Political families reposition themselves. Even some of my own friends are already distracting themselves with the most premature of Philippine political pastimes: Who will be president in 2028? Sara? Someone else? Who can win? Who can defeat whom? Have we learned nothing? We have spent three columns arguing that whoever becomes president enters the same political architecture — one capable of chewing up reformers, accommodating mediocrities, and converting even good intentions into political compromises. Yet here we are again, searching for our next savior before we have finished quarreling over the present one — Leni, Sara, Raffy, Bam — or the actor Robinhood! While Alex was learning to defeat the person across the net, Philippine politics was already deciding who should occupy Malacañang. Apparently, presidential elections are our national version of changing the driver while refusing to repair the car. When government goes underwater Consider the floods. Rain is a natural phenomenon. Flooding may sometimes be unavoidable. But when drainage systems repeatedly fail, projects exist on paper while communities remain underwater, contractors prosper while citizens suffer, and investigations commence only after public outrage, we are no longer discussing meteorology. We are discussing institutions. The same principle applies to impeachment. Whether one supports or opposes Sara is secondary to a larger question: Can our constitutional mechanisms investigate wrongdoing fairly, establish facts credibly and impose accountability without becoming instruments of factional warfare? Strong institutions should investigate a vice president without persecution, defend one without favoritism, punish wrongdoing without vengeance and establish innocence without political accommodation. Otherwise, justice depends upon who controls the machinery. And that is where things become interesting. And who judges the judges? Take Sen. Loren Legarda. Her son, Batangas Rep. Leandro Leviste, built Solar Philippines and secured for his Solar Para sa Bayan a 25-year congressional franchise in 2019. He was a 25-year-old billionaire — kuno! Before approval, the franchise drew objections from energy groups, cooperatives and legislators, who warned of unusual advantages for one company; an ethics complaint alleged Legarda used influence to favor her son’s enterprise. To be fair, Legarda abstained when the Senate voted on the franchise. There is no evidence that she voted to enrich her son. But the matter did not end there. Last July 31, the Ombudsman ordered a preliminary investigation into plunder and graft complaints involving Legarda, Leviste and former energy secretary Alfonso Cusi concerning solar projects and some P10.44 billion in alleged unpaid government obligations. Investigators are examining allegations that Legarda helped her son secure government privileges. Legarda has categorically denied the accusations as false and baseless. She deserves the presumption of innocence. But notice the institutional comedy. A sitting senator facing questions about her own exercise of public influence may nevertheless sit in judgment upon the alleged misconduct of a vice president. And she is hardly alone in inhabiting our strange ecosystem of accusers, accused, investigators and judges. Several politicians associated with controversies surrounding flood control projects have themselves faced allegations or investigations. Yesterday’s investigator can become today’s accused; today’s accused may become tomorrow’s judge. Only in Philippine politics can the players occasionally serve as referees — and then argue about where the goalposts should be. This is not about declaring Legarda or anyone else guilty. It is about a system where legislators grant franchises, political families enter regulated businesses, government agencies supervise privileges politicians themselves created — and eventually politicians sit in judgment upon one another. Build the court, not another savior Which brings me back to Alex. On a tennis court, your mother cannot move the baseline for you. Your surname cannot lengthen the service box. A padrino cannot whisper to the umpire that perhaps 40-love could be reconsidered. The lines existed before Alex arrived. That is what institutions are supposed to mean. Build the court properly. Draw the lines clearly. Establish the rules beforehand. Find competent officials to enforce them. Reward performance. Penalize violations. Then allow human talent to flourish. Alex will win some matches and lose others. Her loss to Bencic actually makes the metaphor better. A functioning system does not guarantee victory. It guarantees a fair opportunity to earn it. That is what millions of Filipinos discover abroad. We keep looking for another president to save the Philippines when perhaps we should finally build a Philippines that does not need saving by a president. We do not need a Republic that promises every Filipino victory. We need a Republic where nobody — president, vice president, senator, dynasty or padrino — gets to move the lines. Alex already has such a court. It is time the Filipino people had one too. lito.lorenzana@cdpi.asia

results.title: David Licauco enters new career chapter with Viva
results.description: Actor and model David Licauco is entering a new phase in his showbiz career after signing a contract with Viva in partnership with ALV Talent Circuit. The partnership, announced Aug. 7, comes as Licauco is now more intentional about the stories and characters he takes on. According to Viva Artists Agency, the actor is eager to work with new creative collaborators and continue developing his craft across film, TV and music. Licauco said he discussed with the Viva team the kinds of projects he hopes to pursue, with some of his suggestions receiving positive feedback. “When we had a meeting at Viva’s office, I mentioned what I wanted to do. And they were really agreeable, saying, ‘Oh, yeah, I think this will suit you,’” Licauco said during a press conference. “They also presented me with a show that I really like. So, yeah, I have a project that I’m really excited about, and on which I’ll do my best.” His dream role One of his biggest ambitions is to headline a Korean drama adaptation. The actor said he wants to maximize the youthful energy associated with romantic and dramatic stories while he still can. “Since I’m getting a bit older, I want to maximize that sense of youth, the youth energy of shows. Let’s say romantic, love, drama. Actually, what I really want to do is a K-drama adaptation,” he said. When asked what kind of Korean drama character he would like to portray, Licauco cited Park Sae-royi (played by Park Seo-joon), the lead character in “Itaewon Class,” a story about ambition, perseverance and building a business from the ground up. He said he connected with the character’s journey of having little to eventually achieving success. “I feel like his life story is somewhat similar to mine. He started from nothing and worked his way up to this height, to everything, through hard work and persistence. So, I feel like our life stories are somewhat similar. That’s why I really want to do it,” Licauco said. Stories over labels With more experience under his belt, Licauco said his priorities have also changed. Rather than focusing primarily on whether he is playing a lead or supporting role, he now pays closer attention to the story. “I wouldn’t say that I’m in control of my career. Maybe now, I just have more awareness of what I want and don’t want to do. Luckily, I’ve been getting projects that I like,” he said. “Before, my questions were really just, ‘Am I the lead there? How much is the talent fee?’ It was mostly things like that. Now, I need to look at what the story really is. It doesn’t matter if I’m the lead, and it doesn’t matter if I’m supporting. I think it’s really the story and what will leave an impression on people,” he continued. For Licauco, the goal is to continue improving rather than be defined by a particular role or image. Asked how he wants to be known as a leading man, he described himself as “versatile.” “I just want to improve with every project I’m part of. So if people think I did a good job in this show, then I’m happy with that,” he said. Staying with GMA Licauco’s move to Viva does not mean leaving GMA, where he remains under Sparkle. He clarified that his upcoming Viva One project is a digital series and that he has received permission to take part in it while maintaining his existing TV commitments. The collaboration also brings together Viva, ALV and GMA’s Sparkle, which showed the growing possibilities for partnerships across entertainment companies. Representatives involved in the project also opened the possibility of future collaborations, including a film involving the three companies should the digital project prove successful. For Licauco, the opportunity is more about making the most of the trust placed in him. “I’m just really happy about the opportunities that I’ve received, and I just want to repay the trust that they’ve given me,” he said. “I’m trying to keep it real, staying in the moment. Sometimes, when you think about the big things happening to you, you can get overwhelmed and you might not be able to perform well,” Licauco continued. “I was a little nervous earlier, but I just thought, I’ll just try to be in the moment. That’s what I do every day,” he added.

results.title: Vietnam’s VinSpace, SpaceX sign deal
results.description: HANOI — Vietnamese aerospace company VinSpace said on Tuesday it has signed a contract with SpaceX to send its first satellites into orbit aboard a SpaceX ride-share mission in 2027, as the Southeast Asian nation moves to develop its nascent space industry. VinSpace will launch its satellites on a SpaceX Transporter ride-share mission run by Elon Musk’s company, which carries satellites from multiple customers on a single rocket to share launch costs, it said in a statement. The satellites, which VinSpace said it will develop and operate, will test the company’s technology in orbit and support future commercial applications. VinSpace is part of Vietnam’s Vingroup conglomerate and was established in November 2025. The company said in April that it planned to develop and launch its first satellites in 2027. Founded by tycoon Pham Nhat Vuong, Vingroup is Vietnam’s largest privately owned company. It has a sprawling business empire that touches many aspects of daily life, from real estate and retail to health care, education and tourism. It is going global as it invests heavily in high-tech industries such as electric vehicles, space, artificial intelligence and robotics, sectors central to Vietnam’s ambition to become Asia’s next tiger economy. Vietnam has sought to build its aerospace capabilities for several decades but remains a relatively small player in the global space industry. It launched its first telecommunications satellite in 2008, followed by another in 2012, according to official documents. In March, it inaugurated a major space science and technology center in Hanoi’s Hoa Lac High-Tech Park, aimed at expanding the country’s satellite development and use of space-based data. Vietnam aims to become a mid-level space power in Southeast Asia by 2030. In February, Vietnam allowed SpaceX to launch its Starlink satellite internet service in the country. This was seen by some analysts as an effort by Vietnam to avoid US tariffs. Starlink has since begun accepting orders in Vietnam. VinSpace said the agreement with SpaceX is part of its plan to become a full-service aerospace company, developing capabilities ranging from satellite design and manufacturing to launch management, satellite operations and space-based data services. “Reliable access to space is fundamental to turning satellite innovation into operational missions,” VinSpace CEO Thu Vu said in a statement.

results.title: Pioneer status boosts Lite Shipping expansion
results.description: THE Maritime Industry Authority (Marina) has officially granted "Pioneering Status Protection" to Lite Shipping Corporation’s newly launched roll-on/roll-off (Ro-Ro) vessel, the M/V Lite Ferry Twenty, recognizing the company's aggressive fleet modernization efforts and its pivotal role in enhancing inter-island connectivity and regional commerce. The incentive, granted under government domestic shipping modernization frameworks, provides pioneer operators with key benefits including six-month route protection, a 50-percent discount on application and renewal fees, and streamlined regulatory processing. Marina Administrator Sonia Malaluan highlighted that the entry of state-of-the-art vessels like the M/V Lite Ferry Twenty extends far beyond mere fleet expansion, serving as a primary driver for trade, tourism, and local economic development across strategic sea corridors connecting Luzon, the Visayas, and Northern Mindanao. Featuring international classification by RINA of Italy, the newly deployed M/V Lite Ferry Twenty is designed to significantly upgrade standard passenger and cargo capacity along the vital Batangas City–Caticlan corridor — linking Luzon directly to Western Visayas and Boracay — while offering enhanced safety systems and broader deck clearance. Lite Shipping Chief Executive Officer Lucio Lim Jr. affirmed that the company's ongoing investments reinforce its commitment to maintaining one of the youngest and safest domestic fleets in the Philippines while actively supporting the government's maritime transportation development goals.

results.title: Capiz under state of calamity
results.description: ILOILO CITY — The province of Capiz was placed under a state of calamity on Monday, following the widespread infestation of the red-striped soft scale insect (RSSI), which has severely affected sugarcane plantations and threatened the livelihood of farmers. The Sangguniang Panlalawigan (Provincial Board) approved the declaration upon the recommendation of Gov. Fredenil Castro, who endorsed the resolution that sought the declaration due to the severe RSSI infestation. The resolution was approved unanimously during a special session of the provincial board on Monday. Data from the Office of the Provincial Agriculturist showed that 3,331.61 hectares of sugarcane plantations had been affected by RSSI as of Aug. 10, involving 1,819 sugarcane planters in 11 local government units (LGUs). The affected areas are in Cuartero, Dao, Dumalag, Dumarao, Jamindan, Maayon, Panitan, Pilar, Pontevedra, President Roxas and Sigma. The provincial government said the declaration would allow authorities to mount a faster and broader response to contain the infestation, protect farmers’ livelihoods and prevent further damage to the province’s sugarcane industry. The declaration came as provincial officials, sugar industry stakeholders, government department heads and private-sector representatives held an emergency summit on Monday to discuss measures to address the worsening RSSI infestation. The summit, led by Castro, brought together members of the Sugar Planters Board of Directors and other stakeholders to discuss strategies to contain the destructive pest and strengthen assistance to affected farmers. The provincial government of Aklan said there is the need for closer coordination between the provincial government and industry stakeholders to speed up the implementation of interventions and pest-control measures. As part of the province’s response, Castro signed an executive order on Aug. 7 creating an RSSI Task Force tasked with leading ­efforts to prevent, control and eventually eradicate the infestation in Capiz. In the province of Iloilo, the invasive sap-sucking pest has affected 962.60 hectares of sugarcane farms across eight LGUs. The affected areas are in Dueñas, Passi City, Badiangan, Dingle, Balasan, Barotac Viejo, Banate and San Enrique. Of these, Banate recorded the largest affec­ted area at 300 hectares, followed by Dingle at 184.50 hectares.

results.title: Tuy bet wins Miss World Philippines-Batangas
results.description: TUY, Batangas — Justice at its truest form is never selective. This, in a nutshell, was what Tuy bet, Danielle Amber Dagami, wanted to impart to our present-day politicians and community leaders to consider so that everyone achieves dignity. That was the gist of Dagami’s response during the question-and-answer segment of the Miss World Philippines Batangas 2026, which she eventually clinched on Sunday, Aug. 9, during the grand coronation night held at Malvar Sports Complex in Malvar town. The actual question for Dagami was “A crown gives you a voice, but purpose gives you direction. If you were to present your beauty with a purpose project to our provincial leaders, how would it address our local economic challenges and earn their support?” Dagami, who represented her native town of Tuy which she described as “short in name, boundless in potential and passion,” cut loose with a convincing reply that mesmerized the crowd at the Malvar venue. Her reply: “Well first of all, If I were to present my BWAP (Beauty With a Purpose) advocacy to our politicians or our dearest leaders, I would simply make it align with my core — competence, humility and compassion. Because whenever I pray for a platform or even this crown, I see to it that I also pray for the humility and sincerity to hold it well. So the aim here is when I talk to these politicians, the common ground that we have is we hold a platform of honor and could influence other people. So what I would do is to present the visible steps to attain equitable and impartial access to security and justice. And that is through making social reform programs that also cater to the grassroots level, the vulnerable, the marginalized and the underprivileged sectors. Because justice at its truest form is never selective. Justice makes dignity attainable for all.” Dagami bested 16 other candidates in the province. She was joined on the stage by Reneé Sta. Teresa of Ibaan, who was adjudged Miss World Philippines–Batangas 2026 Ambassadress; Princess Dianne Ramos of Barangay Ambulong, Tanauan City, who emerged as Miss Island Philippines 2026; Victoria Suri Kopietz of Mataas na Kahoy — Miss World Philippines–Batangas 2026 1st Princess; Stephanie Aleona Roxas of Malvar — Miss World Philippines–Batangas 2026 2nd Princess; and Suchi Kaye Lim of Nasugbu — Miss Island Philippines 2026. Dagami succeeded Miss World Philippines Batangas 2025 Kathleen Dale Casenas of the City of Calaca. Lady Louella Lopez, Mar Reyes and RJ Guererro hosted the event. The pageant’s panel of judges was composed of Arnold Vegrafria, Miss World Philippines Organization national director; Miss Global Philippines 2026 Jayvee Lyn Rolejo; entrepreneur Daphne Espina; VIVA artist/Ginoong Parañaque 2025 Calvin Gutierrez; TV/film actor, print and commercial model David Racelis; fashion designer Allin Bassig; founder and CEO of ONZE Studio Hajie Alejandro; fashion designer Ting Joco; and Mister Gay World 2015 Nomer Yuson. The government of Tuy praised Dagami on her victory, saying, “Your dedication, talent and unique beauty have brought honor not only to yourself but to the entire town of Tuy.” “You are a true inspiration to the youth who continue to dream and strive to achieve their goals,” it added. Dagami, a graduate of Communication Arts, Bachelor of Arts in Communication and currently pursuing her Juris Doctor degree in Pamantasan ng Lungsod ng Maynila Law School, was also Mutya ng Tuy 2024.

results.title: 'TRO on wage hike illegal'
results.description: ​THE University of the Philippines Law Center Workers and Employees Program (UP Law Center-WEP) said that the temporary restraining order (TRO) issued by the Pasig City Regional Trial Court (Pasig-RTC) stopping the implementation of the minimum wage hike in Metro Manila is contrary to law, jurisprudence, and the Constitution. ​“Without rule of law, social justice remains elusive for Filipino workers,” it said, noting that courts cannot simultaneously recognize social justice as a constitutional principle while disregarding the statutory institutions and remedies established to make those rights meaningful. ​The statement was signed by UP Law Center faculty members and lawyers affiliated with WEP, including Prof. Patricia R.P. Salvador Daway, Assoc. Prof. E. (Leo) Battad, and lawyers Arnold De Vera, Marwil Llasos, Jayvy Gamboa, Nathaniel Diaz, and Jasper Frederick Briones. ​It added that the court’s order blocking the wage increase rollout has undermined the statutory system Congress created for setting minimum wages and threatens the constitutional mandate of social justice. ​The Regional Tripartite Wages and Productivity Board-NCR issued Wage Order 27 on June 23, granting workers in all sectors in the National Capital Region a P60 daily minimum wage increase effective July 25, followed by another P25 increase on Jan. 20, 2027. ​The two-stage adjustment would bring the total wage increase to P85, making it one of the most significant recent adjustments to Metro Manila’s minimum wage. ​But it was halted after Readycon Trading and Construction Corp. and R-Il Builders Inc. filed a petition for declaratory relief and sought injunctive relief against its implementation. ​On July 24, the Pasig RTC issued a status quo ante order preventing the wage order from taking effect. Six days later, on July 30, the court issued a temporary restraining order extending the block on implementation until Aug. 13. ​The WEP, however, said the court’s intervention conflicts with an explicit provision of the Labor Code. Article 126, as renumbered, provides that no preliminary or permanent injunction or temporary restraining order may be issued by any court, tribunal, or other entity against proceedings before the National Wages and Productivity Commission or the Regional Boards. ​Instead, the Labor Code provides a specific remedy for parties aggrieved by a wage order: an appeal to the National Wages and Productivity Commission within 10 calendar days from publication. ​“For us, these provisions are clear,” the WEP said, arguing that the statutory appeal mechanism should govern challenges to wage orders rather than judicial intervention through a TRO. ​“The courts cannot arrogate upon themselves a function that is not theirs,” the WEP said, adding that doing so would run counter to the judicial duty to uphold the Constitution and the law.

Jia De Guzman reflects on Alas’ journey
results.description: THE twists and turns that Alas Pilipinas went through in the first leg of the 6th SEA V.Cup eventually became part of a bigger journey that culminated in a historic silver-medal finish. Team captain Jia De Guzman reflected on the team’s struggles and setbacks after Alas Pilipinas secured the Philippines’ first-ever silver medal in the SEA V.Cup. “So the struggle we went through in the first leg? All of it was necessary. The losses, the mistakes, the moments where things didn’t click—it was all part of becoming a better team,” De Guzman wrote on Instagram. “We needed those experiences to learn, build chemistry, and understand what we’re capable of.” The Philippines overcame a gritty Indonesia side, 25-13, 23-25, 25-19, 33-31, last Sunday at the Chiang Mai Gymnasium in Thailand to finish second in the tournament. For De Guzman, the difficult first leg—which saw Alas go winless—was not a setback but an important part of the team’s development. “Every strong team in the world was once given the space to make mistakes, experience losses, and learn from them. We’re no different,” she wrote. “This silver is a beautiful reminder that growth takes time, patience, and a willingness to embrace every part of the journey.” The historic silver marked the Philippines’ first-ever runner-up finish in the SEA V.Cup in both the men’s and women’s divisions. The Alas women had previously collected a string of bronze medals in the regional tournament before finally breaking through with silver in the 2026 edition. “So proud of how far we’ve come, and even more excited for how much more we can become,” De Guzman said. She also thanked her teammates and supporters for standing by the squad throughout its difficult campaign. “Thank you to every member of this team for all your hard work and dedication. Also to everyone out there who has given us unconditional love and support.” De Guzman has also been vocal about the need for changes and reforms concerning national team athletes. She skipped the 2026 Asian Volleyball Confederation (AVC) Women’s Cup in June, where the Philippines was led by veteran Alyssa Valdez and finished eighth.
